phase1.intro:
Every control update you've written so far has been manual. Binding is a price tag that updates itself.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: How does a one-way bind actually work?
dialogue: Every observable JavaFX value is exposed through a *Property() method (valueProperty(), textProperty()). [[key:label.textProperty().bind(otherProperty) is a one-way promise: whenever otherProperty changes, label's text updates automatically]] — no listener to write, no handler to remember.

stickyNote.flavor: ➡️ a one-way promise that updates itself
stickyNote.definition: property.bind(otherProperty) creates a one-way relationship — whenever otherProperty changes, the bound property updates automatically, no handler needed.

dialogue: Call `bindBidirectional()` instead, and the relationship becomes two-way: change either side, and the other follows — exactly what you want when two controls both represent the same underlying value (a Slider and a TextField showing the same number).

stickyNote.definition: bindBidirectional() makes a two-way relationship between two properties — changing either updates the other, useful for e.g. a Slider and TextField sharing a value.

topics.buttonText: What are the restrictions on what I can bind?
dialogue: [[warn:bind() only accepts an ObservableValue, not a raw control or a plain value]] — you bind to the TextField's textProperty(), not the TextField itself. And [[key:once a property is bound, calling setText() directly will throw]], since you'd be fighting the relationship you just declared.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚫 bind to properties, and no manual sets after binding
stickyNote.definition: bind() only accepts an ObservableValue (like textProperty()), not a raw control. A bound property throws if you call its setter directly.

phase1.output: (Window with interactive components showing real-time updates via binding)
phase1.openingDialogue: Binding connects two properties once, and one automatically follows the other — one-way with bind(), two-way with bindBidirectional(). ➡️

phase2.errorMessage:
Test.java:12: error: incompatible types: TextField cannot be converted to ObservableValue<String>
        label.textProperty().bind(field);  // ERROR!
                             ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:incompatible types: TextField cannot be converted to ObservableValue<String>]] — a compile-time error, not a runtime one, which is actually the friendlier failure mode here.

label.textProperty().bind(field) tries to bind directly to the TextField object itself. [[key:bind() expects an ObservableValue — the property, not the control that owns it]]. A TextField is a whole control with dozens of properties (text, prompt text, font, disabled state...); textProperty() is the one specific ObservableValue<String> among all of those that bind() actually knows how to watch. The fix is calling field.textProperty() to get that specific property before passing it to bind().

mcq.question:
You bind label.textProperty().bind(field.textProperty()), then later try label.setText("Hi") directly in your own code. What happens?

A) It works fine — bind() only affects automatic updates, manual ones still work
B) It throws, because a bound property can't be set directly while the binding is active
C) It silently does nothing
D) It breaks the binding permanently and label stops updating from field

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a JavaFX program with:
1. A Slider (0-100, default 50)
2. A ProgressBar that shows the slider value (0.0 to 1.0)
3. A Label that displays the exact value

Use property binding to connect all three components.

Hint: ProgressBar expects 0.0-1.0, Slider gives 0-100.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:a binding doesn't recalculate on some fixed timer]] — it's driven entirely by change notifications. The bound property only updates the instant its dependency actually fires a change event, which is why binding is cheap even with dozens of bound controls on screen: nothing is polled, nothing runs unless something genuinely changed.
